Therefore, all are pure as true emptiness.
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Ultimate emptiness is itself ultimate purity; both purity and emptiness signify the transcendence of all marks.

If this is explained in terms of the mind, it is as the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* says: "Conceptual construction is defilement; the absence of conceptual construction is purity," and so forth; hence it is called "purity."
The text consists of seven sections.
First, the internal body, faculties, and consciousness:

"Because awakening is perfectly luminous" (*jue yuanming gu*) traces back to the previously mentioned cause for manifesting purity; it is through the elimination and dissolution [of delusions] that one attains perfect luminosity.
"Revealing the purity of the mind":
This refers to awakening the deluded mind; within the mind, one had clung to dharmas as real.
Now, seeing the nature of dharmas (*dharmatā*), one realizes that all dharmas are empty; therefore, it is called "purity."
It is like a person who does not recognize the substance of a pearl but merely grasps its blue or yellow color; yet, once they see the maṇi, its color is pure.
This is the same throughout all seven sections.
However, as for the successive steps taken to clarify purity, the meaning will be explained later; for now, we shall analyze and explain the names and essences of these dharmas.
"Mind" (*citta*) is the general characteristic, clarifying that which is my own mind, namely the essence of the *ālayavijñāna*.

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* explains the various distinct names of the eighth consciousness; among these, there are four names that apply across all states, and "mind" (*citta*) is one of them.
In the state of delusion, it is called *ālaya* because it functions as both the storehouse of grasping and the repository of the grasper and the grasped;
now, through the accomplishment of contemplative wisdom, the nature of awakening is perfectly luminous, and thus it is simply termed "mind," with the name *ālaya* being dropped.
Since the mind is already pure, it is identical to the stainless consciousness (*amala-vijñāna*); therefore, the following passage suddenly coincides with the realm of the Buddha.
"Because the mind is pure" reiterates what preceded; all subsequent points follow this same principle.
"Seeing that the objects (*viṣaya*) are pure.
In the subsequent mentions of hearing, cognition, and so forth, all are likewise referred to as "objects.

This means that because of the conceptual grasping of my own mind, one perceives all forms and characteristics; because of this grasping of characteristics, seeing and the other [sensory functions] are themselves objects.

One does not speak of external forms and so forth alone as "objects" (viṣaya), nor does one speak of the faculties (indriya) and consciousness (vijñāna) alone as objects; for there are specific scriptural passages concerning the triad of faculty, object, and consciousness.

Upon examining the essence of these objects of perception and so forth, one finds they are none other than the mind of self-clinging; they are merely designated by distinct names based on the points where errors arise from the grasping of marks.

Furthermore, they do not possess an independent essence apart from the triad of sense-faculties, objects, and consciousness. Thus, one understands that the phenomena of the five aggregates and the "self" within those aggregates are neither different nor identical.

Regarding the phrase "because of the purity of seeing," the word "seeing" alone is cited without mentioning "objects"; this sufficiently demonstrates that it is seeing itself that constitutes the objects, rather than external objects.
The same applies to hearing and the other senses.
"The eye-faculty is pure.
The remaining five [faculties] are to be understood by this same principle.
All six are called "faculties" (*indriya*) because they are the bases upon which consciousness relies and because they are capable of giving rise to consciousness.
The first five [sense organs] each arise from their own seeds and manifest as their own activity; they have pure matter derived from the four great elements as their substance.
The mind-faculty (*manas*) is the seventh consciousness, because it grasps external objects and thereby gives rise to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
"Because the faculties are pure, visual consciousness is pure.
The remaining five [consciousnesses] below should be understood by this same principle.
The reason all are referred to as "consciousness" (vijñāna) is that they differ according to the types of their respective faculties and objects.
The name is established according to the sense faculty (*indriya*) because it possesses five characteristics:
first, consciousness arises necessarily based on the faculty rather than from the object-form (*rūpa*), as seen in cases such as the blind not seeing;

second, the consciousness produced by a faculty necessarily undergoes transformation when the faculty undergoes transformation, just as when the eye-faculty is impaired, one perceives blue as yellow; this is not the case when the form itself is destroyed, for then the consciousness is not destroyed.

Third, consciousness that belongs to the faculties: because it arises by means of the seeds of consciousness following along with the faculties, it is not the case that the seeds of matter follow the seeds of consciousness;

fourth, consciousness that assists the faculties: because when the faculty joins with consciousness, what is experienced by that consciousness causes benefit or harm to the faculty, whereas this does not apply to the objective sphere;
fifth, consciousness that is like the faculties: both the faculty and consciousness are of the nature of sentient beings (*sattva-saṃkhyāta*), whereas that matter is not necessarily a sentient being.
Because the five faculties are preeminent in terms of ultimate reality, they are said to be the bases [of consciousness].
According to the *Awakening of Faith*, all six are termed "mental consciousness" (*manovijñāna*), because these six all arise based upon the mind and are the consciousnesses of the mind.
Therefore, that commentary explains the causes and conditions for arising and ceasing, saying:

"It is because sentient beings revolve in dependence upon mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), and mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). 'Mind' refers to the very substance of the *ālayavijñāna*; 'thought' refers to the five types of thought, because within the two meanings of the *ālaya*, there is the meaning of non-awakening."
Arising without awareness, it is able to see, manifest, and grasp objects, giving rise to a continuous stream of thought.

This consciousness of mental cognition (*manovijñāna*) is precisely this continuous consciousness; based on the increasingly deep attachments of ordinary people, it conceives of a self and what belongs to the self. Following various deluded attachments, it clings to objects according to circumstances and discriminates the six sense-fields. It is called the consciousness of mental cognition, also termed the consciousness of separation, and is further described as the consciousness that discriminates phenomena.
“Because consciousness is pure, the objects of hearing are pure.
Because hearing is pure, the ear faculty is pure.
Because the faculty is pure, ear-consciousness is pure.”
"Because consciousness is pure, the perception of objects is pure.
It is the same for the nose, tongue, body, and mind.
This concludes the preceding explanation.
However, among the eight consciousnesses, the seventh is not explicitly mentioned because its meaning corresponds to the objects of seeing, hearing, and so forth.
By combining the seventh with the eighth, they are termed the "objects of seeing and so forth.
Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"The ālayavijñāna necessarily arises in association with two consciousnesses.

Furthermore, the seventh [consciousness] together with the sixth is called the "perceiver" and so forth regarding objects, because when the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) perceives external objects, it must internally rely upon the manas as its defiled root in order to arise.
Therefore, the aforementioned treatise states:
"Based precisely upon this continuous consciousness, it is even designated as the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

Neither that treatise nor the present sutra lists a separate manas; the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* is likewise, for all [texts] regard the seventh consciousness’s reckoning of the internal as self as corresponding to the aspect of transformation (*pravṛtti-lakṣaṇa*).
Regarding the calculation of external "mine," it is integrated with the *vastu-vijñāna* (object-consciousness).

If one does not connect what precedes with what follows, then the principle of the sequential arising of mental factors (*caitta*) would not be clearly demonstrated, as the meaning would be untenable.
2. The six external sense objects (*viṣaya*).
"Good son! Because the faculties (*indriya*) are pure, the sense object of form (*rūpa-viṣaya*) is pure."
"Because form is pure, the sense-object of sound is pure;
the same applies to odor, flavor, tangibility, and mental phenomena.
These six are all called "dusts" (*rajas*) because they defile and obscure the mind-consciousness; this is spoken in reference to ordinary worldlings.
They are also called the six objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*), which apply to both ordinary beings and noble ones (*ārya*).
Regarding the mention of "form" (*rūpa*) and so forth, this is because they are what is apprehended by the eye and the other sense organs.

Form has both general and specific meanings; here, it refers to the specific meaning, namely that which is apprehended solely by the eye, characterized by visibility (*sanidarśana*) and resistance (*sapratigha*), and possessing the nature of being subject to change and obstruction (*rūpaṇa*). This is because it is the coarsest and most manifest among the objects. Sound and the others may be understood accordingly.
Only the single object of the mental dust (*dharmāyatana*), which is grasped solely by the mind, pervades all [three].
Third, the internal and external four great elements (*mahābhūta*). "Good son!..."
Because the six sense objects are pure, the earth element is pure.
Because the earth element is pure, the water element is pure.
The fire element and the wind element are likewise so.

Thus, regarding the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*), one does not grasp the meaning of the arising of consciousness that draws forth the mind, but directly grasps the substance of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
The *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* states that each of the four great elements is twofold, namely internal and external.
Regarding the earth element, there are two types: internal refers to that which is solid within one's own or another's body, such as hair and body hair;
external refers to that which is solid outside the body, such as earth and wood.
The water element is twofold: that which is internal to the body, consisting of the nature of moisture such as tears and sweat;
and that which is external to the body, consisting of the nature of moisture such as rain and dew.
The fire element is twofold: that which is the internal heat-substance and the characteristic of heat within the body capable of digesting food and drink; and [the external].
Regarding the element of heat (*tejo-dhātu*): the internal body of heat consists of the nature of heat, its characteristics, and its capacity for maturation, and so forth;

the external body of heat consists of movement, transformation, and so forth. Regarding the element of wind (*vāyu-dhātu*), there are two types: the internal body of wind, which is characterized by rapidity and resides in the four limbs and other parts of the body;
and the external body of wind, which consists of motion, turning, and so forth.
4. Worldly Dharmas. "Good son!
Because the four great elements are pure, as previously stated, the twelve bases—the six sense organs and the six sense objects—are the locations where consciousness arises."
Because "bases" (*āyatana*) have the meaning of being gateways for birth, they are also called "persons.
Consciousness is constantly obscured because the sense organs and their objects interpenetrate one another.

As for the "eighteen realms" (*dhātu*), because within the gates of the six sense organs each of the three—organ, consciousness, and object—has its own distinct domain, they also carry the meanings of cause and lineage.
The preceding section was the second hexagram, where the commentator rested in the cessation of karmic causes.
This is the third hexagram, wherein one contemplates the remedy for ego-clinging.
Taken together, these encompass the five aggregates (skandhas) and fully embody the three categories (dhātus).
There are no schools of the Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna that do not rely on this to clarify their various doctrines.

What was previously stated regarding the false identification with the body and mind composed of the four elements, as well as the phrase "the combination of internal and external," refers precisely to the meaning of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*); therefore, these are omitted here.
"The purity of the twenty-five realms of existence.

The four continents, the four miserable destinies, the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments, the realm of non-conception, the Pure Abodes, the Brahma Kings, and the six heavens of desire constitute the twenty-five realms of existence. All of these are "existence" (bhava); each is categorized as such because it pertains to actual retribution and is not subsumed under right wisdom.

However, while the Brahmā King resides in the first dhyāna, the Non-conceptualizers (asaṃjñin) and the Pure Abodes (śuddhāvāsa) reside in the fourth dhyāna; these are singled out from within the stages of the four dhyānas because the Brahmā King possesses views, the Non-conceptualizers belong to non-Buddhists, and the Pure Abodes are exclusively for noble ones (ārya), thus distinguishing them from other devas.
5. Supramundane dharmas. "Because they are pure":
this refers back to the previously mentioned mundane dharmas. Regarding the "ten powers" (*daśabala*):

although the Tathāgata possesses only a single power—the wisdom-power regarding the true nature of all dharmas (*dharmatā*)—this power has ten modes of function, and is therefore described as being tenfold.
The general definition of "power" (*bala*) is that it can crush enemies and cannot be overcome.

First, knowing what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñāna*): this means knowing generally the causes, conditions, and karmic fruits of all phenomena, thereby subduing the notions of no-cause and evil causes; and knowing which persons can be saved and which cannot.

Second, knowing the three types of karma—past, present, and future—and the three types of retribution, such as those corresponding to the present life, thereby knowing whether those to be saved possess obstacles or are free from them.
Third, knowing the defilement and purity of the various dhyānas, liberations, and samādhis, as well as the fruits obtained based upon them;
fourth, knowing the superior, middling, and inferior degrees of the five faculties, such as faith;
fifth, knowing the various inclinations and desires, causing [beings] to abandon the impure and increase the pure.

Sixth, knowing the various dispositions of desire, such as those of the three vehicles, as well as greed, hatred, and delusion; knowing [the timing of] the immediate moment and other times, and who may be delivered and who may not;
seventh, knowing the destination reached by all paths;
eighth, knowing past lives.
Ninth is the knowledge of dying here and being reborn there, which is the wisdom of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*); this alone is named after its basis.
Tenth is the knowledge of one’s own liberation without doubt, as well as the knowledge of sentient beings’ exhaustion of outflows and entry into *nirvāṇa*.

However, the power of the Buddha is immeasurable; yet, for the sake of the conditions through which he delivers sentient beings, he speaks only of ten [powers], which is sufficient to clarify the matter.
Regarding the "four fearlessnesses": first, he correctly knows all dharmas, meaning that the Buddha’s truthful words are: "I am one who possesses all-encompassing right knowledge," and so forth;
second, he has exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*) along with their residual impressions (*vāsanā*), saying: "My outflows are exhausted," and so forth.
Third, he proclaimed all factors that obstruct the path;
fourth, he proclaimed the path for escaping suffering.
The Buddha spoke these four dharmas with truthful words, being resolutely fearless.
"The four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*): because wisdom encounters four objects without obstruction.
First, phenomena (*dharma*), such as earth, water, fire, wind, and so forth;
second, meanings (*artha*), such as solidity, moisture, heat, and motion, and so forth."
The third is eloquence in speech, which refers to obtaining the local dialects of others to explain the stages (*bhūmi*) and so forth;
the fourth is delighting in eloquent discourse regarding the three types of knowledge.
The above is based on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*; however, if one follows the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, the first two differ from this:
That is to say: first, knowing specific characteristics; second, knowing general characteristics.
Furthermore: first, knowing intrinsic nature; second, knowing arising and ceasing. Yet again:
first, the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*); second, inferential knowledge (*anvayajñāna*).
Furthermore, first there is the knowledge of the single characteristic;
second, the knowledge of the aggregates, elements, and so forth.
Again, first there is the knowledge of the equality of the Single Vehicle; second, the knowledge of the distinct natures of the various vehicles.
The latter two are identical in that "eloquence" (pratibhāna) refers to the explanation of the meaning of the Dharma,
whereas "joyful eloquence" (nirukti-pratibhāna) refers to the specific meanings within that eloquence.
This is because while the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (āveṇika-dharma), the powers (bala), and so forth are partially shared with the two vehicles, these [qualities] are not shared at all.

1, 2, and 3 correspond respectively to body, speech, and mindfulness without error; 4 is the absence of divergent thoughts; 5 is the absence of an unconcentrated mind; 6 is the absence of non-knowing when relinquishing; 7 is desire; 8 is diligence; 9 is mindfulness; 10 is wisdom; 11 is liberation; and 12 is the knowledge and vision of liberation. For the first six, it is stated that they are "without decrease. 13, 14, and 15 mean that all bodily, verbal, and mental actions proceed in accordance with wisdom. 16, 17, and 18 mean that through wisdom, one knows the past, future, and present, penetrating them without obstruction.
Question:
"The marks such as the invisible crown of the head are likewise without counterpart; why are they not mentioned? Answer:
"Among these eighteen [dharmas], only the merit of wisdom is explained; the naturally resulting retributive dharmas are not explained.
From the section on the powers (*bala*) up to this point, all four categories are based entirely upon the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
Regarding the "Thirty-seven Factors of Enlightenment" (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*), "assistance" (*pakṣa*) means to provide support, as they assist the right path.
The "path" (*mārga*) is the cause, namely *śamatha* (calming) and *vipaśyanā* (insight).
"Factors" (*dharmāḥ*) refers to categories, as they belong to the same category as the true cause.
They are also called the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*), where "factor" (*pakṣa*) carries the sense of a cause.

The thirty-seven are: the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path.

However, it takes ten factors as its substance: namely, eight each for diligence, concentration, and wisdom; four for mindfulness; three for ethical discipline; two for faith; and one each for pliancy, joy, equanimity, and applied thought.

Regarding the first four foundations of mindfulness: first, one contemplates the body through five kinds of impurity—namely, its seed, its dwelling place, its specific characteristics, its intrinsic nature, and its ultimate state;
second, one contemplates that the three types of sensation are all suffering—namely, painful, pleasant, and neutral sensations;
third, one contemplates that the mind is impermanent from moment to moment.
Fourth, one contemplates that all phenomena are without self;
this serves as the antidote to the four perversions of ordinary beings.
Furthermore, one contemplates that the body is ultimately empty.
Contemplate that feelings are empty internally and externally;
contemplate that the mind is non-existent;
contemplate that phenomena are merely names.
This serves as the antidote to the four inversions of the two vehicles.

Regarding the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*): they are like the fire of the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*); if they obtain the wind of diligence, there is nothing that it does not consume. Therefore, they are established next.
Because its essence is diligence (*vīrya*), it is collectively termed "exertion" (*vīrya*); because it differs from the exertion of non-Buddhists, it is called "right" (*samyak*).
Although it is a single form of exertion, it is divided into four according to its meaning:
first, preventing unarisen evil from arising; [second, abandoning arisen evil; third, generating unarisen good; and fourth, increasing arisen good].
Second, to sever already arisen evils so that they do not continue;
third, to cause unarisen virtues to arise;
fourth, to cause already arisen virtues to expand.
The four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) are: desire, diligence, mind, and investigation.
"Desire" refers to aspiration;
"diligence" refers to uninterrupted application.
"Concentration" (*citta*) refers to meditative absorption (*samādhi*), which is the state of one-pointedness toward a single object;
"contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*) refers to wisdom (*prajñā*), which is internal discernment.
Because diligence that exceeds [the proper measure] leads to distraction and the fire of knowledge becomes feeble, one must establish fixed concentration; this is the mastery over what is desired.
"Divine" (*ṛddhi*) refers to supernormal power, and "feet" (*pāda*) refers to meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Because one can realize this through the four concentrations—desire and so forth—which possess the most supreme mastery over supramundane phenomena, they are called the "bases of divine power" (*ṛddhipāda*); they are also called the "bases of psychic power" (*ṛddhipāda*), because that which is desired accords with the mind.
The five faculties (*pañcendriya*) are faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom; these five collectively give rise to supramundane dharmas (*lokottara-dharma*).
Because they cannot be uprooted by the preceding three categories, these first three [faculties] are collectively designated as "faculties" (*indriya*) when reaching this stage.
The five powers (*pañca-balāni*) are the further development of the aforementioned five faculties (*pañcendriyāṇi*);

Regarding the seven factors of enlightenment: mindfulness is the factor of support, for by means of binding the mind to the object, it ensures that all wholesome dharmas are not forgotten;
the investigation of dharmas is the factor of essential nature, for it realizes their specific characteristics;
and vigor is the factor of deliverance, for by its power one is able to reach the destination.
Joy (*prīti*) is the factor of benefit, because through mental exhilaration the body becomes pliant;

serenity (*praśrabdhi*), concentration (*samādhi*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) are all factors of non-defilement, because they can eliminate heaviness and rigidity (*dausthulya*), because they rely on concentration to effect the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*), and because through the equanimity of practice one permanently abandons both greed and sorrow.

All seven are called factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*). Although these seven factors arise simultaneously in a single moment, their respective functions are explained according to their individual modes of activity (*ākāra*).
Regarding the Eightfold Noble Path: Right View is the factor of discernment, because it discriminates the reality previously realized.

Each of the remaining seven is also termed "right": Right Thought is the factor of instructing others, because one establishes the names and meanings through reflection and gives rise to speech according to what has been realized.

The latter three are all factors for inspiring confidence in others: "speech" refers to providing answers and making determinations based well upon what has been realized, so as to inspire confidence in others regarding the purity of one's view;
"action" refers to physical action, wherein the conduct of movement and stillness is fully perfected, so as to inspire confidence in others regarding the purity of one's ethical discipline;

Vigor is the factor for purifying the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), because through it one is forever separated from all fetters (*saṃyojana*).

Concentration is the factor for purifying the obstacle to supreme qualities, because through it one brings forth immeasurable and superior qualities such as the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

If it were by melting away existence that gold were produced, then even when melting inert stones and the like, one should likewise obtain gold; therefore, we know that although the process of smelting and refining in a furnace is required, the nature of gold must inherently exist.

"Though an infinite time passes, the nature of the gold does not perish" clarifies that while in the ore it is hidden, and once removed from the ore it is manifest; although the hidden and the manifest differ, the nature of the gold is fundamentally equal.
